entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.1-Lev.22.16">Lev 22:1-16</reference> <div eID="gen1450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1451" type="x-p"/> Reverence for Things Sanctified. - The law on this matter was, (1) that no priest who had become unclean was to touch or eat them (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.2-Lev.22.9">Lev 22:2-9</reference>), and (2) that no one was to eat them who was not a member of a priestly family (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.10-Lev.22.16">Lev 22:10-16</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.17-Lev.22.20">Lev 22:17-20</reference> <div eID="gen1459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1460" type="x-p"/> Acceptable Sacrifices. - <reference osisRef="Lev.22.18">Lev 22:18</reference>-20. Every sacrifice offered to the Lord by an Israelite or foreigner, in consequence of a vow or as a freewill-offering (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.7.16">Lev 7:16</reference>), was to be faultless and male, “for good pleasure to the offerer” (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.1.3">Lev 1:3</reference>), i.e., to secure for him the good pleasure of God. An animal with a fault would not be acceptable.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.21-Lev.22.22">Lev 22:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen1460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1461" type="x-p"/> Every peace-offering was also to be faultless, whether brought “to fulfil a special (important) vow” (cf. Num 15:3, Num 15:8 : פּלּא, from פּלא to be great, distinguished, wonderful), or as a freewill gift; that is to say, it was to be free from such faults as blindness, or a broken limb (from lameness therefore: <reference osisRef="Deut.15.21">Deu 15:21</reference>), or cutting (i.e., mutilation, answering to חרוּם <reference osisRef="Lev.21.18">Lev 21:18</reference>), or an abscess (יבּלת, from יבל to flow, probably a flowing suppurating abscess).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.23">Lev 22:23</reference> <div eID="gen1461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1462" type="x-p"/> As a voluntary peace-offering they might indeed offer an ox or sheep that was רקלוּט שׂרוּע, “stretched out and drawn together,” i.e., with the whole body or certain limbs either too large or too small;<note placement="foot">In explanation of these words <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi> very properly remarks, that with the Greeks the sacrificial animal was required to be ἀφελής (<hi type="italic">Pollux</hi> i. 1, 26), upon which <hi type="italic">Hesychius</hi> observes, μήτε πλεονάζων μήτε δέων τι τοῦ σώματος.</note> but such an animal could not be acceptable as a votive offering.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.24">Lev 22:24</reference> <div eID="gen1462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1463" type="x-p"/> Castrated animals were not to be sacrificed, nor in fact to be kept in the land at all. מעוּך <hi type="italic">compressus</hi>, θλιβίας, an animal with the stones crushed; כּתוּת <hi type="italic">contusus</hi>, θλασίας, with them beaten to pieces; נתוּק <hi type="italic">avulsus</hi>, σπάδων, with them twisted off; כּרוּי <hi type="italic">excisus</hi>, τομίας or ἐκτομίας, with them cut off. In all these different ways was the operation performed among the ancients (cf<hi type="italic">. Aristot. hist. an.</hi> ix. 37, 3; <hi type="italic">Colum</hi>. vi. 26, vii. 11; <hi type="italic">Pallad</hi>. vi. 7). “And in your land ye shall not make,” sc., וגו מעוּך, i.e., castrated animals, that is to say, “not castrate animals.” This explanation, which is the one given by Josephus (<hi type="italic">Ant</hi>. iv. 8, 40) and all the Rabbins, is required by the expression “in your land,” which does not at all suit the interpretation adopted by <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi> and <hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>, who understand by עשׂה the preparation of sacrifices, for sacrifices were never prepared outside the land. The castration of animals is a mutilation of God’s creation, and the prohibition of it was based upon the same principle as that of mixing heterogeneous things in Lev 19:19.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.25-Lev.22.26">Lev 22:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen1463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1464" type="x-p"/> Again, the Israelites were not to accept any one of all these, i.e., the faulty animals described, as sacrifice from a foreigner. “<hi type="italic">For their corruption is in them,</hi>” i.e., something corrupt, a fault, adheres to them; so that such offerings could not procure good pleasure towards them. - In <reference osisRef="Lev.22.26-Lev.22.30">Lev 22:26-30</reference> three laws are given of a similar character.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.27">Lev 22:27</reference> <div eID="gen1464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1465" type="x-p"/> A young ox, sheep, or goat was to be seven days under its mother, and could only be sacrificed from the eighth day onwards, according to the rule laid down in <reference osisRef="Exod.22.29">Exo 22:29</reference> with regard to the first-born. The reason for this was, that the young animal had not attained to a mature and self-sustained life during the first week of its existence.<note placement="foot">For this reason the following rule was also laid down by the Romans: <hi type="italic">Suis faetus sacrificio die quinto purus est, pecoris die octavo, bovis tricesimo </hi>(Plin. <hi type="italic">h. n.</hi> 8, 51).</note> <div eID="gen1465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1466" type="x-p"/> This maturity was not reached till after the lapse of a week, that period of time sanctified by the creation. There is no rule laid down in the law respecting the age up to which an animal was admissible in sacrifice. <hi type="italic">Bullocks</hi>, i.e., steers or young oxen of more than a year old, are frequently mentioned and prescribed for the festal sacrifices (for the young ox of less than a year old is called עגל; <reference osisRef="Lev.9.3">Lev 9:3</reference>), viz., as <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.18">Lev 23:18</reference>; Num 7:15, Num 7:21, Num 7:27, Num 7:33, Num 7:39.; Num 8:8; Num 15:24; Num 28:11, Num 28:19, Num 28:27; Num 29:2, Num 29:8, and as <hi type="italic">sin-offerings</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.4.3">Lev 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.4.14">Lev 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.16.3">Lev 16:3</reference>; - <hi type="italic">sheep</hi> (lambs) of one year old are also prescribed as <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings</hi> in <reference osisRef="Lev.9.3">Lev 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.12.6">Lev 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.12">Lev 23:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.29.38">Exo 29:38</reference>; Num 6:14; Num 7:17, Num 7:21, Num 7:27, Num 7:33, Num 7:39., Num 28:3, Num 28:9, Num 28:19, Num 28:27; Num 29:2, Num 29:8, Num 29:13, Num 29:17., as <hi type="italic">peace-offerings</hi> in Num 7:17, Num 7:23; Num 29:35., and as <hi type="italic">trespass-offerings</hi> in Num 6:12; also a yearling <hi type="italic">ewe</hi> as a sin-offering in <reference osisRef="Lev.14.10">Lev 14:10</reference> and Num 6:14, and a yearling <hi type="italic">goat</hi> in Num 15:27. They generally brought older oxen or bullocks for peace-offerings (Num 7:17; Num 23:29.), and sometimes as burnt-offerings. In Jdg 6:25 an ox of seven years old is said to have been brought as a burnt-offering; and there can be no doubt that the goats and rams presented as sin-offerings and trespass-offerings were more than a year old.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Lev.22.28-Lev.22.30">Lev 22:28-30</reference> <div eID="gen1466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1467" type="x-p"/> The command not to kill an ox or sheep at the same time as its young is related to the law in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.19">Exo 23:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.22.6-Deut.22.7">Deu 22:6-7</reference>, and was intended to lay it down as a duty on the part of the Israelites to keep sacred the relation which God had established between parent and offspring. - In <reference osisRef="Lev.22.29">Lev 22:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.22.30">Lev 22:30</reference>, the command to eat the flesh of the animal on the day on which it was offered (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.15">Lev 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.19.5-Lev.19.6">Lev 19:5-6</reference>) is repeated with special reference to the praise-offering.
entries.content_plain:
Lev 22:28-30 
 
 The command not to kill an ox or sheep at the same time as its young is related to the law in Exo 23:19 and Deu 22:6-7, and was intended to lay it down as a duty on the part of the Israelites to keep sacred the relation which God had established between parent and offspring. - In Lev 22:29, Lev 22:30, the command to eat the flesh of the animal on the day on which it was offered (Lev 7:15; Lev 19:5-6) is repeated with special reference to the praise-offering.
